messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Karim's Story

Karim was fifty-four when he first sat across from a therapist, his shoulders hunched forward as if bracing against an invisible force. He had been married to David for eighteen years—a partnership that had felt, until three years ago, like the safest place he had ever known. What happened in that relationship had fractured something fundamental in him, something he had only recently admitted he needed help to repair.

The violence had come gradually, then suddenly. David's criticisms had started as corrections—the way Karim folded laundry, the tone he used with his mother on the phone, his tendency to spend too much time organizing community events instead of being present at home. By the time the first blow landed, Karim had already begun to believe he deserved it. The assault had occurred in their bedroom on a winter evening. David had been drinking, and Karim had made the mistake of suggesting they talk about his behavior. What followed was a sustained attack—fists, then objects, then David's voice, low and venomous, telling him exactly what he was: selfish, ungrateful, a failure. The sounds of that night lived in Karim's head now, unbidden and vivid. He would hear David's breathing, harsh and rhythmic, or the specific timbre of his voice saying words Karim could no longer quite remember but whose emotional weight remained crushing. Sometimes a helicopter passed overhead—the kind that occasionally flew over the city—and the sound would transport him completely. His body would go rigid. He would be back in that room, unable to move.

After he left David, Karim had tried to continue his work as a community organizer, coordinating housing initiatives and social services for vulnerable populations in the neighborhood. But the office where he had spent so many productive years began to feel impossible. The building was only three blocks from the apartment he and David had shared, and he found himself unable to walk past it. He would take elaborate detours, adding twenty minutes to his commute, his heart rate climbing as he approached the vicinity. Eventually, he stopped going to that office altogether. He worked from home when he could, but his supervisor had begun to ask questions about his availability. The work that had once defined him, that had given him a sense of purpose and contribution, had become something he could only do in fragments.

Karim had also begun to dress differently. He wore dark, oversized clothing—heavy sweaters in summer, jackets that obscured his frame. He kept his head down in public spaces. There was a logic to this that made sense to him: if he was invisible, if he took up less space, perhaps no one would notice him. Perhaps no one would hurt him. He had come to believe that something about him—something intrinsic to who he was—had made him vulnerable to David's violence. He was the kind of person who could be hurt this way. The world, he had learned, was not a place where love was safe. Trust was a luxury he could no longer afford. People were dangerous, and the only reliable protection was constant vigilance and withdrawal.

What had finally brought him to seek help was a panic attack at the grocery store. A man had stood too close behind him in the checkout line, and Karim's body had simply shut down. He couldn't breathe. He couldn't move. An employee had to call an ambulance. Sitting in the emergency room, waiting for his heart rate to return to normal, Karim had felt the full weight of what his life had become. He was isolated, afraid, and increasingly unable to function in the most basic ways. His marriage to David was over, but David's presence had not left him. The trauma lived in his body, in the darkness of his bedroom, in the sound of aircraft, in the careful architecture of avoidance he had constructed around his life. Karim was hoping that someone could help him find his way back to himself—the person who had once believed in community, in connection, in the possibility of safety. He was afraid that person no longer existed.
